en: A Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Maṇḍala of the Seventeen Holy Ones,
including the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva of True Reality and the Samādhi of Non-empty Great Bliss,
from the Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra, in one fascicle.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daixingshan Monastery—Grand Master of the Court (Kaifu Yitong Sansi), Special Advancement (Teshen), Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Shi Honglu Qing), Duke of Su Commandery with a fief of three thousand households, recipient of the purple robe, posthumously titled Minister of Works (Sikong), and conferred the posthumous name Dajian (Great Mirror)—in accordance with imperial decree, and with a brief preface based on his exegesis. At that time, the Tathāgata Vairocana...
In the palace of the king of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations,
for the sake of the great bodhisattvas and others,
he taught this profound principle of the Prajñāpāramitā through the seventeen gates of pure phrases.
This is indeed the meaning of the mantras of the seventeen bodhisattva samādhis.
In order to cause those who can maintain them to swiftly attain bodhi,
he then expounded these secret words spoken by the Tathāgata and the various great beings regarding the great maṇḍala of the seventeen noble stages.
By practicing in reliance upon this, one will swiftly achieve accomplishment.
What are the seventeen holy ones?
The first is the Bodhisattva Mahāsukhā-amogha-samaya-tattva-vajra.
This represents the body of all Buddhas and Samantabhadra,
which pervades the receptacle world and the world of sentient beings;
it is so named because its boundless sovereignty is eternal in principle, its essence is quiescent, and it is neither false nor subject to destruction.
Holding the vajra bell in the left hand signifies the meaning of delight;
its placement at the left of the waist symbolizes the Great Self (Mahātman).
Holding the five-pronged vajra in the right hand signifies the meaning of the five wisdoms.
Turning the fist outward signifies showing it to sentient beings.
Within the maṇḍala, he occupies the central position and encompasses all the various forms.
Aside from these, there are sixteen positions;
these constitute the path to perfect enlightenment.
The second of these is the so-called Mind-born Vajra Bodhisattva.
With the arrow of great compassion,
he destroys the minds of those of the two vehicles;
this is why he holds this arrow in his hand.
Yet he manifests as the Body of Wisdom of Equality, which is free from both [extremes] and like an illusion;
this is what is called Kīlikīla-vajra-bodhisattva,
which in the language of the Central Kingdom is named "Contact" (sparśa).
Because he does not abandon sentient beings and ensures their certain liberation;
because he wishes to clarify that the nature of contact is itself bodhi;
for these reasons, he abides in the posture of embracing.
And he manifests the body of wisdom of the equality of purity and illusion through touch.
These four are the Bodhisattvas of Compassionate Vajra;
because of their compassion, [they act thus].
With the rope of loving-kindness,
they universally bind all sentient beings; until they have reached Bodhi,
they never abandon them.
It is also like the great makara fish that swallows whatever it encounters;
once something has entered its mouth, there is no escape.
For this reason, we carry this banner of the makara fish.
Yet he manifests the wisdom-body of the equality of illusion, wherein attachment, bondage, renunciation, and abandonment are all equal;
this is the so-called fifth, the Bodhisattva Vajramāna, who,
by means of unsurpassed wisdom, [performs this].
To cause all sentient beings to fully realize the essence of Vairocana Tathāgata and to attain mastery over both the mundane and supramundane realms,
he dwells in an air of majestic pride.
Yet he manifests the wisdom-body of the equality of both self and non-self as an illusion.
His six [aspects] are those of the Bodhisattva Vajradarśana, who,
with the eye of great wisdom that is quiescent yet illuminating, [perceives].
Within the realm of affliction and the wondrous pure land, up to the ultimate and conventional truths,
one perceives only the truth of the supreme meaning and reality of all phenomena,
without distraction or movement.
Thus, by holding the seal of the mind-born,
one manifests the body of samādhi;
the seventh is the so-called Bodhisattva Vajraprīti.
One attains the purity of physical pleasure within the sensory objects;
one neither loathes nor dwells in saṃsāra, yet remains liberated from it.
This is why he holds the vajra-mark of touch.
He manifests the body of that samādhi;
the eighth is so-called because the Bodhisattva Vajrarāga attains purity through passion itself.
Thus, by means of greed, one is able to accumulate all merit and wisdom and swiftly realize bodhi;
this is because one abides in the nature of greedy attachment.
Therefore, by holding the mudrā of compassion,
he manifests his body of samādhi;
the ninth is the so-called Bodhisattva Vajreśvara.
Moving freely through the three realms with sovereign fearlessness,
one attains the essence of the Great Self within both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
for this reason, one abides in the mark of adamantine pride.
And he manifests the body of that samādhi.
Its ten [emanations] are as follows: the Bodhisattva Vajraspring, who is able to give rise to clouds and oceans of offerings from the flowers of bodhi-awakening.
Furthermore, by means of skillful means, he bestows it upon sentient beings to create merit and benefit;
as flowers are the business of spring,
he consequently names it after them.
Therefore, he also holds a flower as his mudrā.
The eleventh is the Bodhisattva Vajramegha,
who is able to use the compassionate clouds of the Dharma’s moisture.
It moistens and nourishes all sentient beings;

furthermore, through skillful means, it takes the foul impurities and unwholesome states of their bodies and minds since beginningless time and transforms them into immeasurable clouds of fragrant incense for offering.
Because the incense smoke from his brazier resembled clouds,
he took that as his name;
thus, he held the incense burner as his seal of commitment.
The twelfth is the Bodhisattva Vajraśarad,
who constantly destroys all darkness with the lamp of wisdom and bestows it upon sentient beings through skillful means.
He gave rise to an ocean-like cloud of offerings of immeasurable light;
because its empty color was as clear and refreshing as autumn,
it was intended to symbolize the essence of the light of wisdom.
Thus he was named accordingly;
therefore, he held a lamp as his seal of commitment (*samaya*).
He is the thirteenth, known as the Bodhisattva Vajra-Hima (Vajra Frost/Snow).
One is able to smear the essence of the minds of sentient beings with the fragrance of the five untainted aggregates (anāsravaskandha),
thereby extinguishing the foul heat of their afflictions (kleśa).
They accomplish the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body and,
through skillful means, bestow it upon sentient beings,
giving rise to ocean-like clouds of offerings of fragrant ointments.
Because the sandalwood unguent dispels all poisonous heat like frost and snow,
it was named accordingly;
thus, one holds the unguent as its mudrā.
The fourteenth is the so-called Bodhisattva Vajrarūpa.
By means of the wisdom of pure form,
he manifests a body of enjoyment within the Pure and Sublime Realm.
Within the realm of affliction (*saṃkleśadhātu*), one manifests transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) for the purpose of gathering [beings] in; therefore,
the hook is taken as the seal (*mudrā*).
The fifteenth is the Bodhisattva Vajrasvara.
By means of the wisdom of pure sound,
he is able to manifest sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voices.
It serves as the means for universally pervading the *dharmadhātu* and introducing [beings] therein;
thus, one holds the cord as a seal (*mudrā*).
This is the sixteenth, known as the Bodhisattva Vajragandhā.
By means of the fragrance of pure wisdom,
one produces the fragrance of the natural renown of the Vajradhātu;
this enters all distracted minds to serve as the practice of *śamatha*.
Therefore, holding a chain is taken as the mudrā.
The seventeenth is the so-called Bodhisattva Vajrarasa,
who [employs] the wisdom of the purity of taste.
Taking the supreme flavor of the yoga-samādhi as one's source of joy,
one holds the bell as a mudrā.
Such great bodhisattvas possess these seventeen kinds of pure samādhi-wisdom.
Based on the text, they are described in detail;
there are immeasurable gates concerning names, meanings, essences, functions, principles, phenomena, accomplishments, and realizations.
This is merely a rough presentation of the general outline.
It is an abridged summary of the essential meaning from the thirteenth assembly of the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, titled the *Great Samaya-Truth Yoga*.

A Commentary on the Meaning of the Great Maṇḍala of the Seventeen Holy Ones, including the Bodhisattva Vajrasatya, based on the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra*, the Great Blissful and Unfailing Samādhi, in One Scroll.
